screens.title: Developing Stream Analytics Queries (SAQL)
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how Stream Analytics Query Language, SAQL, extends standard S Q L to handle continuous, unbounded streams of events. We'll build from simple filtering and projections to time-windowed aggregations and joins. You will also learn how to handle mixed data types and when to use CAST or TRY_CAST to avoid runtime errors. The skills here matter because streaming queries run continuously and must be precise about timestamps, windows, and types to produce accurate, timely results. For example, using a Tumbling window to compute average temperature every five minutes gives you periodic summaries, whereas a Sliding window helps detect bursts of events as they occur. We'll also cover stream-to-stream joins for correlating events between feeds, and enriching streams with reference data. By the end of this chapter you'll be comfortable writing SAQL queries that filter, aggregate, join, and cast data while following practical best practices that keep jobs efficient and reliable. Think about a sensor network: correct timestamping, sensible window sizes, and safe casts determine whether you detect anomalies or miss them. Ready to explore the building blocks and patterns you will use in real jobs?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will write SAQL queries that filter and project streaming fields, apply appropriate windowing functions to aggregate over time, and join streams or enrich events with reference data. You will also safely convert and validate types so that aggregates like average and sum operate only on numeric values. These objectives matter because streaming pipelines operate continuously; small mistakes in window definitions or type handling can cascade into incorrect alerts or wasted compute. For example, using TRY_CAST lets you filter out malformed strings before applying AVG, preventing job errors and skewed metrics. Another concrete outcome is the ability to choose Tumbling, Hopping, Sliding, or Session windows depending on whether you need non-overlapping periodic summaries, rolling moving averages, event-triggered detection, or grouped sessions with gaps. Finally, you'll learn key practices to monitor Streaming Units and keep queries efficient. These skills let you build reliable, interpretable streaming analytics that power dashboards and alerts in real time.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Validation
screens.narratorSegment: You will practice by authoring queries, testing them with sample or live input in the Query editor, and verifying outputs in your configured Blob output. The hands-on activity in this chapter walks you through writing a basic filter and a tumbling window aggregation, then starting the job to observe JSON output. Practically, you will run a filter that selects temperature readings above a threshold and a tumbling window that computes average temperature and event counts. This practice matters because breaking queries into small, testable steps reduces runtime surprises. For instance, test your WHERE clause first with sample JSON before adding GROUP BY and HAVING. Also validate type conversions using TRY_CAST to exclude malformed values. Finally, monitor SU utilization and job lateness when you run the job with live input; these indicators show whether your window sizes and joins are causing delays. This approach builds confidence: write small queries, test them, then combine them into production-ready streaming jobs.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Practice & Validation
Practice steps
A simple cycle to validate streaming queries
1. Author
Write small queries: a filter, then a basic aggregation, then a join. Keep each step focused.
2. Test

screens.title: SAQL basics: SELECT, FROM, WHERE
screens.narratorSegment: SAQL starts from familiar S Q L foundations: SELECT, FROM, and WHERE. In streaming contexts these clauses run continuously against incoming events, producing results as new events match the criteria. A common pattern is to alias an input such as an Event Hub stream and then select fields you need, for example deviceId, temperature, and humidity. Filtering with WHERE reduces downstream processing and storage by excluding irrelevant events early. A concrete example is selecting temperature readings above 25 degrees to route high-temperature telemetry to an alerting pipeline. A common misconception is to assume streaming WHERE clauses only run once; they evaluate for every arriving event in real time. Also be mindful that outputs often include System. Timestamp to indicate the event processing or window end time — this helps downstream systems align results. When building queries, start with a simple SELECT/FROM/WHERE and test with sample input to ensure fields and types match your expectations. This approach reduces debugging complexity before adding windows or joins. How might you validate that your WHERE filters are not unintentionally discarding edge cases? SAQL basics: SELECT, FROM, WHERE means select/from/where run continuously on streams — start simple, filter early, and include system.timestamp when helpful.. In practical terms, project fields and filter streaming events the familiar way. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › SAQL basics
SELECT, FROM, WHERE
A continuous projection and filter pipeline
SELECT
    deviceId,
    temperature,
    humidity,
    System.Timestamp AS EventProcessingTime
FROM
    TelemetryInput TIMESTAMP BY EventEnqueuedUtcTime
WHERE
    TRY_CAST(temperature AS float) IS NOT NULL
    AND TRY_CAST(temperature AS float) > 25
Why TRY_CAST?
Avoids errors when temperature sometimes arrives as a string. Filters keep aggregates valid.
Quick test
Upload sample JSON to the Query editor and verify outputs before starting the job.
Explanation & Example
  • SELECT chooses only needed fields to reduce downstream traffic and storage.
  • FROM references the streaming input; TIMESTAMP BY defines which timestamp to use for windows.
  • WHERE filters each arriving event in real time; test with sample input to validate logic.
Key Takeaway

Start queries simple: filter bad types, validate with sample data, and include timestamp fields so outputs are time-aware.

Check your understanding
How would you confirm your WHERE clause does not drop edge-case values such as nulls or strings that should be numeric?

screens.title: Windowing fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Windowing is the mechanism that turns an unbounded stream into bounded slices suitable for aggregation and pattern detection. Without windows you cannot compute sums, averages, or counts over a meaningful period because streams are infinite. The key idea is to group events that fall within a time interval and then compute aggregates for that interval. Tumbling windows give fixed, non-overlapping buckets; hopping windows produce overlapping buckets for moving averages; sliding windows emit results whenever events enter or leave the time span; and session windows group events separated by short gaps into a single session. A common misconception is to treat window size as purely technical — window size encodes your business cadence. For example, a five-minute tumbling window summarizes activity every five minutes, suitable for dashboards. In contrast, a sliding or hopping window helps with burst detection and smoothing. Always pair window choice with the analytic goal and watch for late or out-of-order events: correct TIMESTAMP BY usage is essential to ensure events are assigned to the right windows. Windowing fundamentals means windows create bounded groups from continuous events so you can compute aggregates across time intervals aligned with your analytic goals.. In practical terms, why temporal windows are necessary for unbounded streams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Windowing fundamentals
Why windows matter
Windows turn infinite streams into bounded groups for aggregation and pattern detection.
Window types — quick map
  • Tumbling: fixed, non-overlapping. One event belongs to exactly one window.
  • Hopping: fixed size but overlapping; hops forward by a period for moving averages.
  • Sliding: outputs when events enter or exit, good for burst detection.
  • Session: groups events into sessions separated by gaps beyond a timeout.
Analytic examples
Periodic reports: Tumbling windows for hourly metrics.
Moving average: Hopping window, e.g., 5-minute window every minute.
Burst detection: Sliding window to alert on sudden surges of events.
Sessionization: Session windows to assemble user activity with gaps.
Misconception
Window choice is not just technical. Choose it to match the business question and latency requirements.
Key Takeaway
Map your analytic goal to the right window type before tuning sizes or hop intervals.

screens.title: Tumbling windows
screens.narratorSegment: Tumbling windows are fixed-length, contiguous, and non-overlapping intervals. Each event maps to exactly one tumbling window, which makes them ideal for periodic summaries such as minutes, hours, or daily aggregates. The typical SAQL pattern uses TUMBLINGWINDOW and a GROUP BY with TIMESTAMP BY to align events correctly. For example, to compute average temperature every five minutes you would group by deviceId and TUMBLINGWINDOW(minute, 5). Use System. Timestamp in the SELECT to report the window end time so downstream systems know the period represented by the aggregate. A common mistake is forgetting TIMESTAMP BY and assuming events will be grouped by the correct time; without TIMESTAMP BY ASA defaults to the enqueued time but your events might carry a more accurate timestamp field. Another pitfall is choosing a window size that is too large, which delays insights, or too small, which increases output volume and compute. Start with the business reporting cadence and test with sample data to validate that events fall into expected buckets. Tumbling windows means use for fixed periodic summaries; ensure correct timestamp alignment and sensible window size for latency and cost.. In practical terms, fixed-size, non-overlapping intervals for periodic aggregation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Tumbling windows
TUMBLINGWINDOW example
Fixed, contiguous buckets for periodic metrics
SELECT
    System.Timestamp AS WindowEnd,
    deviceId,
    AVG(TRY_CAST(temperature AS float)) AS AverageTemperature
FROM
    TelemetryInput TIMESTAMP BY EventEnqueuedUtcTime
GROUP BY
    deviceId,
    TUMBLINGWINDOW(minute, 5)
Outcome
Every five minutes you'll get one aggregate per device with WindowEnd indicating the interval end.
Pitfall
Very small tumbling windows increase output frequency and SU usage; choose size to balance latency and compute.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm TIMESTAMP BY points to the correct field.
  • Decide window size by reporting cadence and latency needs.
  • Test with sample input to ensure expected assignment to windows.
Key Takeaway

Tumbling windows are predictable and easy to reason about; use them when you need periodic summaries.

screens.title: Hopping windows
screens.narratorSegment: Hopping windows are fixed-size windows that advance by a hop period smaller than the window length, producing overlapping intervals. This overlap lets you compute moving averages or smoothed metrics at a chosen cadence. For example, a HOPPINGWINDOW(minute, 5, 1) produces a five-minute window every minute, producing overlapping aggregates that approximate a moving average. This is useful when you want frequent updates that incorporate recent history. When constructing hopping windows, remember that overlapping means more outputs and higher SU utilization; each event can belong to multiple windows. Also, interpret outputs carefully: consecutive outputs will include many of the same events, so downstream consumers should know these are overlapping aggregates. Test performance by running queries with realistic event rates to observe SU usage. A common mistake is setting the hop too small compared to the window, generating excessive outputs. Choose hop frequency to match the cadence of your dashboard or alerting needs and monitor resource use. Hopping windows means use hopping windows to compute moving averages with overlapping intervals; tune hop period to balance freshness and compute cost.. In practical terms, overlapping windows for moving averages and smoothing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Hopping windows
HOPPINGWINDOW pattern
Overlapping windows for regular rolling summaries
SELECT
    System.Timestamp AS WindowEnd,
    AVG(TRY_CAST(temperature AS float)) AS MovingAverageTemperature
FROM
    TelemetryInput TIMESTAMP BY EventEnqueuedUtcTime
GROUP BY
    HOPPINGWINDOW(minute, 5, 1)
When to use
Dashboards needing frequent refreshed trends, where each update uses multiple minutes of history.
Performance note
Overlapping windows increase SU usage. Measure and adjust hop size to control output volume.
Key Takeaway
Hopping windows trade extra compute for smoother, more frequent insights.

screens.title: Sliding windows
screens.narratorSegment: Sliding windows emit outputs whenever events enter or exit the window interval. They are useful for detecting patterns or bursts tied to event activity rather than fixed time ticks. For example, SLIDINGWINDOW(second, 10) counts events in the last ten seconds and can trigger when EventCount exceeds a threshold. Because sliding windows react to each event, they are particularly good at near-instantaneous pattern detection. A common misconception is that sliding windows are simply smaller tumbling windows; in practice they are event-driven and can produce far more outputs. Use HAVING to filter noisy results, for instance only alert when the event count within the sliding window exceeds a threshold. Test with realistic event streams because sliding windows can increase SU consumption and output rate. When you need immediate detection of sequences or bursts, sliding windows often provide the responsiveness you need. Sliding windows means sliding windows give event-level responsiveness for burst detection but can increase output frequency and su usage.. In practical terms, event-driven sliding windows for burst detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Sliding windows
SLIDINGWINDOW example
Event-driven counts for immediate detection
SELECT
    System.Timestamp AS WindowEnd,
    COUNT(*) AS EventCount
FROM
    TelemetryInput TIMESTAMP BY EventEnqueuedUtcTime
GROUP BY
    SLIDINGWINDOW(second, 10)
HAVING
    EventCount > 50
Use case
Detect traffic spikes or rapid sequences like error bursts within short intervals.
Misconception
Don't confuse sliding with tumbling. Sliding outputs more frequently and is event-driven, not fixed-tick.
Key Takeaway
Choose sliding windows when you need immediate, event-driven detection of changing conditions.

screens.title: Session windows
screens.narratorSegment: Session windows group events that belong to the same activity separated by small idle gaps. They are ideal for sessionization tasks, like user activity or device interactions that may pause and resume. A session window starts with the first event and continues until a configured inactivity timeout elapses, then a new session begins. For instance, SESSIONWINDOW(minute, 5, 1) can be used to end a session if no events arrive for five minutes, with an additional parameter controlling late arrival tolerance. The main benefit of session windows is they reflect natural interaction boundaries rather than fixed clock periods. A common pitfall is setting the inactivity timeout too small, splitting logically continuous sessions, or too large, merging unrelated sessions. When you need to understand user journeys or device sessions over irregular periods, session windows provide a natural grouping aligned to behavior instead of calendar ticks. Session windows means use session windows to group related events separated by small gaps, giving natural activity-driven groupings for analysis.. In practical terms, group events into sessions that tolerate gaps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Session windows
SESSIONWINDOW behavior
Capture activity groups that tolerate gaps between events
SELECT
    System.Timestamp AS WindowEnd,
    deviceId,
    COUNT(*) AS SessionEvents
FROM
    TelemetryInput TIMESTAMP BY EventEnqueuedUtcTime
GROUP BY
    deviceId,
    SESSIONWINDOW(minute, 5, 1)
When to choose
User sessions, device interaction periods, or transaction groups with intermittent activity.
Tune carefully
Set inactivity timeout to reflect expected pauses. Too small splits sessions; too large merges unrelated activity.
Key Takeaway
Session windows mirror real interaction patterns and are essential for behavioral analytics.

screens.title: Aggregations and built-in functions
screens.narratorSegment: Aggregations in SAQL work much like S Q L: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX compute statistics over grouped events, and you use them inside a GROUP BY with a window to create time-based summaries. Built-in functions for strings, math, and dates let you transform fields before aggregation. For instance, use TRY_CAST to convert temperature strings to floats before AVG, filtering out non-numeric values to avoid skewed results. Another typical pattern is combining AVG and COUNT with HAVING to output only meaningful summaries, for example only windows with at least two events. Use functions to prepare data, then aggregate inside windows

screens.title: Joins in SAQL
screens.narratorSegment: SAQL supports both stream-to-stream joins and stream-to-reference joins. Stream-to-stream joins correlate events from two live inputs based on a common key and a time relationship. An example is joining telemetry to alerts within a five-second window to correlate cause and effect. These joins require TIMESTAMP BY on both streams and a DATEDIFF (or similar) clause to bound the join by time. Stream-to-reference joins enrich live events with static or slowly changing lookup data, like device metadata stored in Blob or S Q L. This is useful for adding location or owner fields to events without performing external lookups per event. A misconception is to assume reference joins scale like stream joins; reference joins are efficient but the reference data should be reasonably sized and configured as a reference input. Stream-to-stream joins can be expensive: they increase SU usage and require careful time bounds to avoid large, unbounded state. Use stream-to-reference for enrichments and stream-to-stream only when correlation within short time windows is required. Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Joins in SAQL
Stream-to-stream vs Stream-to-reference
Choose joins based on correlation needs and reference sizes
Stream-to-stream example
SELECT
  t1.deviceId,
  t1.temperature,
  t2.alertMessage
FROM
  TelemetryInput t1 TIMESTAMP BY EventEnqueuedUtcTime
JOIN
  AlertStream t2 TIMESTAMP BY EventEnqueuedUtcTime
ON
  t1.deviceId = t2.deviceId
  AND DATEDIFF(second, t1, t2) BETWEEN -5 AND 0
Stream-to-reference example
SELECT
  t.deviceId,
  t.temperature,
  r.location
FROM
  TelemetryInput t TIMESTAMP BY EventEnqueuedUtcTime
JOIN
  DeviceReferenceData r
ON
  t.deviceId = r.deviceId
Performance note
Bound stream joins in time to limit state. Large, unbounded joins increase SU consumption.
Key Takeaway
Prefer reference joins for enrichment and short, time-bounded stream joins for correlation.

screens.title: Type handling: CAST and TRY_CAST
screens.narratorSegment: SAQL is strongly typed for many functions, and data from event producers can arrive with inconsistent types. Fields like temperature or pressure may come as strings or numbers depending on the producer. Using CAST or the safer TRY_CAST prevents runtime errors and ensures only valid values contribute to aggregates. TRY_CAST returns NULL when conversion fails, letting you filter invalid values with a WHERE clause before computing AVG or SUM. For example, first filter WHERE TRY_CAST(temperature AS float) IS NOT NULL, then compute AVG(TRY_CAST(temperature AS float)). A common error is to call AVG on a field that sometimes contains non-numeric strings; this produces NULL aggregates or job errors. Another pattern is to use COALESCE to provide defaults after casting, but be careful because defaults can bias averages. Test with representative sample inputs, and log or inspect dropped values to understand whether casting filters are discarding important data. This approach keeps aggregates meaningful and jobs stable in production. screens.title: Best practices & monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Production streaming queries must be maintainable and observable. Favor simple queries: break complex logic into multiple ASA jobs if necessary. Complex operators, many joins, and large windows increase state and Streaming Unit consumption, which can cause lag. Monitor SU utilization, job lateness, and output rate; these metrics tell you whether your job is keeping up. When you see high SU usage, consider: reducing window sizes, simplifying joins, or splitting logic across chained jobs. Also explicitly use TIMESTAMP BY with a reliable timestamp field in your events to ensure correct window assignment. Late or out-of-order events can be handled by adjusting allowed lateness or by using session windows that tolerate gaps, but be mindful of the extra state required. Finally, validate your queries with sample input and small live tests before running at full scale. These practices help maintain low-latency, accurate streaming analytics. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how Stream Analytics Query Language, SAQL, extends standard S Q L to handle continuous, unbounded streams of events. We'll build from simple filtering and projections to time-windowed aggregations and joins. You will also learn how to handle mixed data types and when to use CAST or TRY_CAST to avoid runtime errors. The skills here matter because streaming queries run continuously and must be precise about timestamps, windows, and types to produce accurate, timely results. For example, using a Tumbling window to compute average temperature every five minutes gives you periodic summaries, whereas a Sliding window helps detect bursts of events as they occur. We'll also cover stream-to-stream joins for correlating events between feeds, and enriching streams with reference data. By the end of this chapter you'll be comfortable writing SAQL queries that filter, aggregate, join, and cast data while following practical best practices that keep jobs efficient and reliable. Think about a sensor network: correct timestamping, sensible window sizes, and safe casts determine whether you detect anomalies or miss them. Ready to explore the building blocks and patterns you will use in real jobs?

By the end of this chapter you will write SAQL queries that filter and project streaming fields, apply appropriate windowing functions to aggregate over time, and join streams or enrich events with reference data. You will also safely convert and validate types so that aggregates like average and sum operate only on numeric values. These objectives matter because streaming pipelines operate continuously; small mistakes in window definitions or type handling can cascade into incorrect alerts or wasted compute. For example, using TRY_CAST lets you filter out malformed strings before applying AVG, preventing job errors and skewed metrics. Another concrete outcome is the ability to choose Tumbling, Hopping, Sliding, or Session windows depending on whether you need non-overlapping periodic summaries, rolling moving averages, event-triggered detection, or grouped sessions with gaps. Finally, you'll learn key practices to monitor Streaming Units and keep queries efficient. These skills let you build reliable, interpretable streaming analytics that power dashboards and alerts in real time.

You will practice by authoring queries, testing them with sample or live input in the Query editor, and verifying outputs in your configured Blob output. The hands-on activity in this chapter walks you through writing a basic filter and a tumbling window aggregation, then starting the job to observe JSON output. Practically, you will run a filter that selects temperature readings above a threshold and a tumbling window that computes average temperature and event counts. This practice matters because breaking queries into small, testable steps reduces runtime surprises. For instance, test your WHERE clause first with sample JSON before adding GROUP BY and HAVING. Also validate type conversions using TRY_CAST to exclude malformed values. Finally, monitor SU utilization and job lateness when you run the job with live input; these indicators show whether your window sizes and joins are causing delays. This approach builds confidence: write small queries, test them, then combine them into production-ready streaming jobs.

SAQL starts from familiar S Q L foundations: SELECT, FROM, and WHERE. In streaming contexts these clauses run continuously against incoming events, producing results as new events match the criteria. A common pattern is to alias an input such as an Event Hub stream and then select fields you need, for example deviceId, temperature, and humidity. Filtering with WHERE reduces downstream processing and storage by excluding irrelevant events early. A concrete example is selecting temperature readings above 25 degrees to route high-temperature telemetry to an alerting pipeline. A common misconception is to assume streaming WHERE clauses only run once; they evaluate for every arriving event in real time. Also be mindful that outputs often include System. Timestamp to indicate the event processing or window end time — this helps downstream systems align results. When building queries, start with a simple SELECT/FROM/WHERE and test with sample input to ensure fields and types match your expectations. This approach reduces debugging complexity before adding windows or joins. How might you validate that your WHERE filters are not unintentionally discarding edge cases? SAQL basics: SELECT, FROM, WHERE means select/from/where run continuously on streams — start simple, filter early, and include system.timestamp when helpful.. In practical terms, project fields and filter streaming events the familiar way. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Windowing is the mechanism that turns an unbounded stream into bounded slices suitable for aggregation and pattern detection. Without windows you cannot compute sums, averages, or counts over a meaningful period because streams are infinite. The key idea is to group events that fall within a time interval and then compute aggregates for that interval. Tumbling windows give fixed, non-overlapping buckets; hopping windows produce overlapping buckets for moving averages; sliding windows emit results whenever events enter or leave the time span; and session windows group events separated by short gaps into a single session. A common misconception is to treat window size as purely technical — window size encodes your business cadence. For example, a five-minute tumbling window summarizes activity every five minutes, suitable for dashboards. In contrast, a sliding or hopping window helps with burst detection and smoothing. Always pair window choice with the analytic goal and watch for late or out-of-order events: correct TIMESTAMP BY usage is essential to ensure events are assigned to the right windows. Windowing fundamentals means windows create bounded groups from continuous events so you can compute aggregates across time intervals aligned with your analytic goals.. In practical terms, why temporal windows are necessary for unbounded streams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Tumbling windows are fixed-length, contiguous, and non-overlapping intervals. Each event maps to exactly one tumbling window, which makes them ideal for periodic summaries such as minutes, hours, or daily aggregates. The typical SAQL pattern uses TUMBLINGWINDOW and a GROUP BY with TIMESTAMP BY to align events correctly. For example, to compute average temperature every five minutes you would group by deviceId and TUMBLINGWINDOW(minute, 5). Use System. Timestamp in the SELECT to report the window end time so downstream systems know the period represented by the aggregate. A common mistake is forgetting TIMESTAMP BY and assuming events will be grouped by the correct time; without TIMESTAMP BY ASA defaults to the enqueued time but your events might carry a more accurate timestamp field. Another pitfall is choosing a window size that is too large, which delays insights, or too small, which increases output volume and compute. Hopping windows are fixed-size windows that advance by a hop period smaller than the window length, producing overlapping intervals. This overlap lets you compute moving averages or smoothed metrics at a chosen cadence. For example, a HOPPINGWINDOW(minute, 5, 1) produces a five-minute window every minute, producing overlapping aggregates that approximate a moving average. This is useful when you want frequent updates that incorporate recent history. When constructing hopping windows, remember that overlapping means more outputs and higher SU utilization; each event can belong to multiple windows. Also, interpret outputs carefully: consecutive outputs will include many of the same events, so downstream consumers should know these are overlapping aggregates. Sliding windows emit outputs whenever events enter or exit the window interval. They are useful for detecting patterns or bursts tied to event activity rather than fixed time ticks. For example, SLIDINGWINDOW(second, 10) counts events in the last ten seconds and can trigger when EventCount exceeds a threshold. Because sliding windows react to each event, they are particularly good at near-instantaneous pattern detection. Session windows group events that belong to the same activity separated by small idle gaps. They are ideal for sessionization tasks, like user activity or device interactions that may pause and resume. A session window starts with the first event and continues until a configured inactivity timeout elapses, then a new session begins. For instance, SESSIONWINDOW(minute, 5, 1) can be used to end a session if no events arrive for five minutes, with an additional parameter controlling late arrival tolerance. The main benefit of session windows is they reflect natural interaction boundaries rather than fixed clock periods. A common pitfall is setting the inactivity timeout too small, splitting logically continuous sessions, or too large, merging unrelated sessions. When you need to understand user journeys or device sessions over irregular periods, session windows provide a natural grouping aligned to behavior instead of calendar ticks. SAQL supports both stream-to-stream joins and stream-to-reference joins. Stream-to-stream joins correlate events from two live inputs based on a common key and a time relationship. An example is joining telemetry to alerts within a five-second window to correlate cause and effect. These joins require TIMESTAMP BY on both streams and a DATEDIFF (or similar) clause to bound the join by time. Stream-to-reference joins enrich live events with static or slowly changing lookup data, like device metadata stored in Blob or S Q L. This is useful for adding location or owner fields to events without performing external lookups per event. A misconception is to assume reference joins scale like stream joins; reference joins are efficient but the reference data should be reasonably sized and configured as a reference input. SAQL is strongly typed for many functions, and data from event producers can arrive with inconsistent types. Fields like temperature or pressure may come as strings or numbers depending on the producer.
